memo:
### Position read
The opponent opened by moving Red from (0,3) to center square (3,3). We answered with Blue from (3,7) to (3,4), occupying the adjacent center and blocking their center-victory route. No losses or eliminations.

### Our plan
Keep at least one secure piece in the center to deny occupation. Develop Green toward (4,3) or (4,4) while seeking a same-color sandwich against the advanced Red at (3,3). Watch all four center squares every turn and favor moves that create paired same-color anchors.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent’s first move was an immediate central claim, suggesting an aggressive center-occupation plan.

### Lessons
Sandwiches require matching colors, so Blue and Green cannot flank together. Moving into a sandwich is safe; only the mover’s landing triggers its captures.

### Position read
The opponent holds center squares (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; we hold (3,4) with Blue. Green moved from (5,0) to (5,4), safely staging beneath the remaining empty center square (4,4). No losses or eliminations.

### Our plan
On Blue’s next turn, strongly consider moving Blue from (4,7) to (4,4), giving us both right-hand center squares while preserving Blue at (3,4). Use Green at (5,4) as nearby reinforcement, but watch for friendly-fire lines because Blue and Green do not flank together. Maintain at least one center square at all times.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent has committed both colors immediately to adjacent left-hand center squares, indicating a direct center-occupation strategy.

### Lessons
Do not place Green at (3,2) or (4,2): the opponent could immediately sandwich it using their center anchor and an edge piece landing at column 1. Staging one row below the center avoids that tactic.

### Position read
The opponent holds (3,3) and (4,3). Our former piece at (3,4) was sandwiched by the move to (3,5), giving our acting color 1 loss. We now have pieces at (4,5) and (5,4); the latter blocks the opponent’s direct route up column 4. No colors are eliminated.

### Our plan
Avoid (4,4) while the opponent retains the anchor at (4,3), since a landing at (4,5) by their lower color would sandwich that piece. Use (4,5) as a safer staging point and preserve the column-4 blockade. If the opponent shifts from (4,3) to (4,4), consider occupying the vacated (4,3) with our edge piece from (4,0). Continue denying complete center occupation before seeking captures.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is pursuing the center aggressively and immediately exploited a same-color sandwich across a center square.

### Lessons
Adjacent opposing center anchors make direct occupation tactically dangerous. Check whether an opponent can land on the opposite side of any proposed center piece before committing it.

### Position read
The opponent occupies (3,3) and (4,4), while we hold (4,3), (4,5), and (5,4). Our acting color has just contested the center without making a capture. Losses: one for our right-edge color, zero otherwise; no eliminations.

### Our plan
The urgent threat is a sandwich of (4,3): the opponent can move from (7,2) to (4,2), using (4,4) as the far flank. On our next turn, block that route by moving our piece from (6,7) to (6,2), provided it remains legal. Maintain (4,3) to prevent center occupation, then seek a way to dislodge (4,4).

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent aggressively occupies central squares and exploits same-color flanks immediately when available.

### Lessons
A contested center piece may be defensible by blocking the attacker’s travel lane rather than retreating. Recheck the planned (6,7)→(6,2) blockade after the intervening move.

### Position read
The opponent holds (3,3), (3,4), and (4,4); we hold (4,3), (4,5), and (5,4). We moved our right-edge piece to (6,2), blocking the opponent’s (7,2) piece from reaching (4,2) and sandwiching our piece at (4,3). Losses: one for our right-edge color, zero otherwise; no eliminations.

### Our plan
Keep (4,3) occupied to deny center victory. Watch for alternate same-color flanks against it and seek a capture or forced displacement of the opponent’s (4,4) piece. Our pieces at (4,5) and (5,4) give useful pressure around that square but cannot pair across colors.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent aggressively occupies central squares and looks for immediate same-color sandwich geometry.

### Lessons
Always identify the moving color and far-flank color before judging a sandwich. Blocking a rook’s travel lane can preserve a critical center defender without retreating.

### Position read
We used the same-color flank at (5,4) to capture the opponent’s pieces at (3,4) and (4,4) by landing at (2,4). The opponent now retains only (3,3) among the four center squares, while we hold (4,3). Our right-edge color has two losses and will be eliminated upon its next capture; the opponent’s two colors now have one loss each.

### Our plan
Preserve (4,3) unless moving it also prevents an immediate center takeover. Use the new piece at (2,4) together with (5,4) to control column 4 and seek further same-color sandwiches. Protect our vulnerable right-edge pieces, especially against captures that would trigger elimination, while recognizing Void pieces would still count for center occupation.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent aggressively occupies the center and uses same-color sandwich lanes, including clearing or exploiting approach squares.

### Lessons
Mixed opponent colors can be captured in one sandwich when an unbroken line lies between two pieces of the moving color. Recheck long alignments through the center before settling for a merely defensive move.

### Position read
We hold (4,3), while the opponent holds (3,3); the other two center squares are empty. We captured two center pieces last cycle, leaving both opponent colors at one loss. Our right-edge color remains critically vulnerable at two losses. Its pieces now stand at (1,7), (3,7), (5,7), and (6,2).

### Our plan
The piece newly placed at (3,7) has a clear horizontal route toward (3,4), so use it to contest the center if the lane remains open. On our intervening turn, our other color can occupy whichever of (3,4) or (4,4) the opponent leaves available, using (2,4) or (5,4). Preserve (4,3) and avoid exposing any right-edge piece to a one-move capture that would cause elimination.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent aggressively contests the center and may use one color to open lines for the other. Expect a blocking move on row 3 or occupation of (4,4).

### Lessons
At two losses, every possible sandwich and enclosure involving our vulnerable color must be checked before moving. Empty gaps break sandwiches, so central occupation and lane control are currently more realistic than an immediate capture.

### Position read
We now hold both lower center squares, (4,3) and (4,4), while the opponent holds (3,3); (3,4) is empty. The opponent’s piece at (3,5) blocks our right-edge piece’s direct route toward the center. Our vulnerable color remains at two losses, with pieces at (1,7), (3,7), (5,7), and (6,2).

### Our plan
Preserve the blocker at (2,4) and contest the upper center without risking our vulnerable color’s final loss. Watch whether the opponent moves its (3,3) piece into (3,4) or reinforces the top-center pair. Seek a safe way to dislodge or contain those pieces while retaining both lower center squares.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is aggressively occupying and obstructing central lanes, most recently placing a piece at (3,5). Expect an immediate challenge at (3,4) or an attempt to attack our central Green pieces.

### Lessons
Central routes must be recalculated after every blocker move. At two losses, check every possible sandwich and enclosure against our vulnerable color before committing it.

### Position read
We hold (4,4); the opponent holds (3,3), while (3,4) and (4,3) are empty. Our vulnerable color has two losses and pieces at (1,7), (3,7), (5,4), and (6,2). The move to (5,4) creates a pincer threat against the opponent piece at (5,3).

### Our plan
Threaten (6,2) to (5,2), which would sandwich and capture (5,3) against our piece at (5,4). Use the forced response to regain central tempo. On our other color’s turn, consider reclaiming (4,3) or occupying (3,4), depending on the opponent’s intervening move, while preserving (4,4).

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent is contesting the center aggressively and just used the aligned pieces at (3,3) and (5,3) to capture our piece at (4,3). Expect an attempt to occupy (3,4), evacuate (5,3), or disrupt our pincer.

### Lessons
A piece that voluntarily enters an existing sandwich is safe, but a flank can later move away and return to retrigger capture. With one color at two losses, verify every immediate sandwich and enclosure before moving it.

### Position read
We hold (4,4); the opponent holds (3,3) and (3,4). Green has moved from (2,4) to (2,3), creating two sandwich threats. Our vulnerable color remains at two losses, with pieces at (1,7), (3,7), (5,4), and (6,2).

### Our plan
The opponent’s first color must address the threat of (4,4) to (4,3), capturing (3,3) against Green at (2,3), or accept that loss. Blue can then play (6,2) to (5,2) if Red remains at (5,3), capturing it against Blue at (5,4). The opponent’s other color must evacuate (3,4) before Green returns to (2,4).

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent prioritizes central occupation and recently entered an existing sandwich safely. Expect both central pieces to retreat if possible, sacrificing tempo to answer the fork.

### Lessons
A single setup move can create independent same-color sandwich threats from two landing squares. Track which opposing color gets an intervening turn before each threat is executed.

### Position read
We hold Green at (4,4). The opponent holds Red at (3,3),(4,3) and Yellow at (3,4). Blue has two losses, so moved its exposed piece from (5,4) to (5,3), avoiding Yellow’s immediate (7,4)->(6,4) sandwich. Blue pieces are now (1,7),(3,7),(5,3),(6,2).

### Our plan
Yellow must consider evacuating (3,4), which Green at (2,3) can capture by moving to (2,4) against Green (4,4). Blue now threatens a future (1,7)->(1,3): the downward line Green (2,3), Red (3,3),(4,3), Blue (5,3) would be sandwiched, costing Red two pieces and eliminating it. On Green’s turn, preserve (2,3) and move another Green unless a stronger capture appears.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent blocks landing squares to neutralize direct captures and prioritizes central occupation. Expect Yellow to leave (3,4), then Red to break the column-three line by moving either central Red piece.

### Lessons
At two losses, check every enemy sandwich before pursuing tactics. A threatened friendly-fire line can still be valuable when it would simultaneously eliminate an opposing color.

### Position read
We hold Green at (4,4), blocking center occupation. The opponent has Red at (3,3),(4,3) and Yellow at (2,4). Blue has two losses; its pieces are (1,7),(3,7),(5,3),(6,2). Green pieces are (1,5),(2,3),(3,0),(4,4),(6,0).

### Our plan
Green (1,5) threatens (2,5), which would sandwich Yellow (2,4) against Green (2,3). Preserve Green (2,3): it also enables Blue (1,7)->(1,3), whose downward sandwich against Blue (5,3) would take Green (2,3) plus both central Reds, eliminating Red. Red must break that column before Blue acts. Keep Green (4,4) in place unless a decisive capture appears, since it denies center victory.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent responds to direct sandwich threats and prioritizes central occupation. Expect Red to move one piece out of column 3, then Yellow to move or block the threatened (2,5) landing square.

### Lessons
Layer threats across consecutive colors. Friendly fire is acceptable when it simultaneously eliminates an opposing color, but Blue’s next move must still account for its two-loss vulnerability.

### Position read
Our Blue pieces are now (1,2),(1,7),(3,7),(5,3), with two losses; avoid any capture. Our Green holds (1,5),(2,3),(3,0),(4,4),(6,0). The opponent has central pieces at (3,3),(4,3), while our (4,4) blocks center victory. Red’s new (3,6), together with (0,4), enables tactical play on column 6.

### Our plan
Preserve Blue (1,7), Blue (5,3), and Green (2,3). If Green (1,5) clears row 1, Blue (1,7)->(1,3) sandwiches Green (2,3) and both central opposing pieces against Blue (5,3), eliminating the opponent’s one-loss color at the cost of one Green. The opponent’s bottom color moves before Green and must answer the threat Green (1,5)->(2,5) against (2,4). Keep Green (4,4) unless there is a forced win.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent prioritizes central occupation and just moved an edge piece to (3,6) without breaking the column-3 structure. Expect the piece at (2,4) to sidestep or occupy (2,5), followed by a central defender moving once Green clears row 1.

### Lessons
Do not move Blue (1,7) to (1,6): the opponent can place a piece at (2,6), then move from (0,4) to (0,6) and sandwich both against the far piece at (3,6), eliminating Blue.

### Position read
Our moved piece is at (1,3); our other Green pieces are (3,0),(4,4),(6,0). Both our colors have two losses, so any further loss eliminates that color. The opponent holds (3,3),(4,3), while our (4,4) prevents center victory. Our Blue anchors are (1,2),(1,7),(3,7),(5,3).

### Our plan
If (2,3) remains empty, move Green (1,3)->(2,3). Then Blue (1,2)->(1,3) sandwiches that Green plus the opposing pieces at (3,3),(4,3) against Blue (5,3), eliminating Green and the opponent’s one-loss Red while preserving Blue. Do not move Blue onto (1,3) before the line is complete. Keep Green (4,4) unless a forced result supersedes the center blockade.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent favors center occupation and should now consider vacating a column-3 piece or occupying (2,3) to disrupt the staged sandwich. Watch for the right-side Red piece moving into (3,4).

### Lessons
Captures only trigger on landing, so the Blue flanker must wait. Avoid placing our two-loss pieces between same-colored opposing anchors; especially avoid (0,5), (3,2), and an unattended piece at (1,6).

### Position read
We shifted our spare piece safely to (0,7), preserving the key pieces at (1,2) and (5,3). Our piece at (1,3) still needs to advance to (2,3). The opponent occupies three center squares; our (4,4) blocks immediate center victory. Both our colors remain one loss from elimination.

### Our plan
If (2,3) is empty on our next turn, play (1,3)->(2,3). After the opponent's reply, aim for (1,2)->(1,3): the downward sandwich through our (2,3) and opposing (3,3),(4,3), ending at our (5,3), eliminates one of our colors but also the opponent color owning both central pieces. Reassess if either central column-3 piece moves or (2,3) is occupied. Keep (4,4) as the center blockade unless a forced win overrides it.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent prioritizes the center and recently reinforced (3,4). Expect disruption by occupying (2,3), moving a column-3 piece, or capturing the blocker at (4,4).

### Lessons
Do not move the (1,2) flanker before (1,3) vacates and the full line is formed. Protect every piece of our two-loss colors from immediate sandwiches.

### Position read
We now have the intended column-3 formation: our Green at (2,3), opposing Red at (3,3) and (4,3), and our Blue at (5,3). Blue at (1,2) can potentially land on (1,3) to capture the entire line. Both our colors remain at two losses; Red has one loss and Yellow has one. Our (4,4) continues to block the opponent’s center occupation.

### Our plan
After the opponent’s Red move, if (1,3) remains empty and the column-3 line still ends with our Blue at (5,3), play Blue (1,2)->(1,3). This captures Green plus both Reds: Green is eliminated, but Red reaches three losses and is also eliminated. Recalculate if Red moves either central piece, moves onto (1,3), dislodges (5,3), or creates an immediate tactical capture. Preserve (4,4) as the center blockade.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent prioritizes center control and should now recognize the column-3 sandwich threat. Expect Red to break the line, occupy (1,3), move the far Blue flanker if capturable, or attack the center blocker.

### Lessons
Before executing the sandwich, verify every square in the line and ensure the landing move is unobstructed. Trading one endangered color to eliminate an opposing color is favorable when it also clears two center pieces.

### Position read
The opponent broke the former column-3 tactic by moving Red from (3,3) to (3,1). We placed Blue at (5,4), forming a prospective column-4 sandwich: empty (1,4), opposing Yellow (2,4), opposing Red (3,4), our Green (4,4), and our Blue (5,4). Losses remain: ours two each; opposing Red and Yellow one each.

### Our plan
If the column-4 chain survives through the next opposing and our turns, Blue can move (1,2)->(1,4), capturing Yellow, Red, and Green. This would eliminate both Green and Yellow while raising Red to two losses. Expect Yellow (2,4) or Red (3,4) to move and recalculate. Preserve (4,4) unless a clearly stronger capture or forced defense appears.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent recognized and dismantled the earlier long sandwich immediately. Expect the current column-4 threat to force Yellow away first, or Red to break the line later.

### Lessons
Long mixed-color sandwiches are useful forcing threats even when the opponent escapes: they dictate which central piece must move. Always verify the entire line remains unbroken before executing.
